title: [HashiCorp] Building a secure foundation for AI on Kubernetes with HashiCorp Vault
summary: AI is moving beyond experimentation and into production, but security controls aren’t necessarily keeping pace. Recent IBM research shows 48% of surveyed executives say their organizations lack adequate protection for model inference and live AI usage, while 56% say the same about AI development and training. As organizations move AI applications, models, and autonomous agents into production environments orchestrated by platforms such as Kubernetes, closing that security gap requires looking beyond the AI model itself.This shift is reflected in team priorities and thought leadership, including the agenda at this year’s KubeCon. Moving a model from demo to production introduces challenges across compute, GPU utilization, model serving, networking, storage, observability, cost and most importantly, security. Autonomous AI agents add the consideration: how can workloads safely and securely interact with infrastructure, APIs, tools, and data. For platform and security teams, that changes the conversation. Securing AI on Kubernetes isn't only about protecting a model or application. It requires securing the infrastructure underneath it, including the data stored by Kubernetes, the identities and certificates workloads use to establish trust, and the credentials applications need to access other systems. Protect the Kubernetes foundation beneath AI workloadsKubernetes uses etcd as its backing store for cluster data, which can include Kubernetes Secrets and other sensitive configuration associated with workloads running in the cluster. By default, the Kubernetes API server stores unencrypted representations of resources in etcd unless encryption at rest is configured. For organizations running sensitive workloads, including AI applications, protecting this data adds an important layer of defense if unauthorized access to the underlying storage occurs. Vault Kubernetes Key Management reduces this risk by integrating Kubernetes encryption with the Vault Transit secrets engine. The vault-kube-kms process exposes the Kubernetes KMS v2 interface and connects the Kubernetes API server to Vault, where the Transit engine is used for cryptographic key wrapping operations.With Vault 2.2, Vault Kubernetes Key Management advances to full support for general Kubernetes deployment. This approach helps organizations centralize control over the keys protecting Kubernetes data rather than managing encryption independently for every cluster.For production AI environments, Kubernetes hosts far more than just the model itself. Model-serving infrastructure, AI gateways, MCP servers, agents, application services, and the configuration required to operate them may all depend on the Kubernetes control plane. Securing AI starts with securing the platform it runs on.Automate trust with Vault and cert-managerAs cloud native architectures become more distributed, applications increasingly rely on certificates to establish trusted, encrypted connections between workloads. Consider an agentic application running on Kubernetes. An AI agent might communicate with an MCP server, which connects to an internal API, which in turn accesses a database or another service. Each connection creates another trust relationship that platform teams need to secure.This web of interdependent services makes automated certificate lifecycle management a critical part of the Kubernetes security model.A new external Vault issuer for cert-manager means application developers can continue requesting certificates using standard cert-manager Certificate resources, while VSO 2.0 sends approved certificate requests to Vault PKI for signing. The approach also reuses VSO's existing authentication and client infrastructure rather than requiring teams to establish a separate Vault integration for certificate management. And with shrinking certificate lifecycles, integrations with Vault and automations in it are even more relevant for teams when it comes to managing certificates. The benefit is not a new certificate workflow. It leverages familiar Kubernetes-native workflows, so that teams that have standardized on cert-manager can continue using these familiar workflows, while bringing certificate signing under centralized Vault PKI controls. This centralized control helps platform teams automate workload trust without asking every application team to learn a separate security process, ensuring identity-based access and secure execution supporting autonomous workload access. Keep secrets synchronized as workloads changeSecret delivery is only part of the problem. Credentials also rotate, applications scale, and configurations change. Common polling approaches can leave a window for downtime between when a credential changes and when a workload receives that change.Vault 2.2 expands Vault Secrets Operator instant updates. VSO 1.6 can immediately deliver changes for dynamic, auto-rotating, and manually rotated database, KV, Azure, and LDAP secrets. VSO reconciliation through Vault event notifications is triggered immediately on secrets changes. Reducing the gap between credential rotation and availability helps security controls keep pace with the applications they protect, which is necessary for dynamic applications, including AI and agentic workloads that interact with multiple services and must move securely at machine speed. Give workloads secure access without the full Vault server footprintSecrets present another challenge. Applications, AI services, and autonomous agents all need credentials to access databases, APIs, cloud services, model endpoints, and other tools at runtime. But the component consuming those secrets doesn't need all the functionality required to operate a Vault server.Vault 2.2 introduces Vault Client. Vault Client packages Vault Agent, Vault Proxy, and a limited set of Vault CLI commands without requiring the complete Vault server binary. Not all organizations have embraced Kubernetes secrets. For deployments and secrets that require additional isolation or more-limited secrets visibility, Vault Agent and Agent Sidecar Injector are now available in a smaller footprint for workloads that need client-side Vault functionality while establishing a clear separation between the capabilities required to operate Vault and those required to consume services from it. For increasingly dynamic cloud native environments, that distinction can help simplify how Vault functionality is deployed alongside applications.Build a security foundation for cloud native AIBut the bigger story is not any individual Kubernetes integration. It's how these capabilities work across different layers of the cloud native stack:Protect cluster data: Vault Kubernetes Key Management connects Kubernetes KMS with Vault Transit to protect Kubernetes data stored in etcd. Establish workload trust: The Vault issuer for cert-manager brings Vault PKI into familiar Kubernetes certificate workflows.Keep credentials current: VSO instant updates help Kubernetes applications receive secret changes as they happen.Secure runtime access: Vault Client provides a lightweight way for workloads to use common Vault client functionality. Together, these capabilities point toward a consistent security model: Kubernetes-native workflows for developers and platform teams, backed by centralized controls for secrets, certificates, and encryption.Secure what comes after the AI demoOrganizations focused on securing AI at scale are challenged beyond just getting a model to run securely in production. Teams need the infrastructure and operational practices to serve models, operate agents, secure workloads, control access, and connect the growing number of systems surrounding AI applications. Security must evolve alongside that infrastructure.As organizations bring AI applications and autonomous workloads onto Kubernetes, Vault can help provide the security foundation beneath them, protecting Kubernetes data, automating workload trust, and giving applications secure access to the credentials they need. Ready to secure your Kubernetes workloads? Explore the HashiCorp Vault Kubernetes developer documentation to get started.

title: [CNCF] Your runtime security tool is not your baseline: Silos dressed as autonomy in cloud native teams
summary: A deadline creates pressure, and a team decides to solve its part of the problem directly. I once saw this play out in a Kubernetes security initiative. The team had capable engineers, a clear objective and a reasonable concern that asking for help might slow them down. They picked a runtime detection tool, deployed it across the clusters and had a dashboard full of events within a week. The missing piece was not the tool. It was the baseline: the shared definition of what normal looks like for those workloads and what should be blocked rather than just reported. Without it, every alert raised the same question: is this expected? The people who could answer that sat in another team, and nobody had asked them early enough. The decision made sense from where the team stood. They had a task, a tool and a plan. What they lacked was the cross-team agreement that makes the tool useful, and confidence that asking for it would get a timely answer. In cloud native engineering, “we can handle this ourselves” sounds like healthy ownership, and often it is. This post is about the cases where it isn’t, and about the artifact that usually exposes the difference: the security baseline. The new version of the silo The old silo was a wall. The new one can be a door that closes without anyone noticing: the team keeps moving and reports progress, but a key conversation never happens. SignalOld siloNew siloLanguage“That is not my job”“We can handle this ourselves”PresenceNobody shows upThe team shows up, does not askFailure modeWork never startsWork starts, then stalls at the missing pieceCostLate, visiblyLate, after looking like progress Autonomy is not automatically a silo. A team that owns its platform and makes its own decisions is what good engineering looks like. The silo appears when autonomy turns into self-sufficiency: the team stops checking who else holds part of the answer and rebuilds knowledge that already exists elsewhere in the organisation. Renaming a team does not fix this either. Platform security, cloud native security and DevSecOps are labels; collaboration still depends on how people work together. Three things make the new silo likely: Deadlines reward visible progress. A deployed DaemonSet and a dashboard are easy to show. Agreeing on expected behaviour, exception handling and verification is less visible, but it decides whether the deployment means anything. Security looks like an approval queue. If every question to a security team turns into a review and a long wait, a well-run engineering team will reasonably try to work around it. That is a design problem for security teams, not a character flaw in platform teams. Prevention is hard to measure. Shipping independently is easy to demonstrate. An early conversation that prevents rework produces a problem that never happens. A tool working as configured is not a control The risk is rarely that a tool fails. It is that a tool works exactly as configured, without a shared understanding of what it is supposed to achieve. The pattern repeats across the cloud native security stack: A runtime detection engine such as Falco ships with general-purpose rules. Turning its output into signal requires knowing what each workload is expected to do, and that knowledge lives with the teams that build and run those workloads. An admission controller such as Kyverno or OPA Gatekeeper can block or only report. Choosing between those modes is a risk decision, not a configuration detail. Kubernetes audit logging produces evidence only if someone has decided what to record, how long to keep it and who reads it. None of these are shortcomings of the projects. They are design dependencies: the tool provides the mechanism, and the organisation has to provide the intent. The baseline is a cross-team artifact A baseline is not a policy document. It is a short, testable set of answers, and every answer maps to something you can configure and verify in a cluster. The question that matters is who has to agree on each one. Baseline questionWhere it lives in the clusterWho has to agreeWhich workloads may run, and with which security context?Pod Security Standards via Pod Security Admission, or equivalent admission policiesPlatform and securityWhich registries and image provenance are accepted?Signature verification with Sigstore enforced at admission (for example Kyverno verifyImages or the Sigstore policy-controller)Security and application teamsWhat is blocked, and what is only reported?Kyverno Enforce or Audit; Gatekeeper deny, warn or dryrun; Pod Security Admission enforce, warn or auditSecurity defines, platform operatesWhat does normal runtime behaviour look like?Falco rules, lists, macros and rule exceptions tuned per workloadApplication teams, with securityWho can approve an exception, and when does it expire?Kyverno PolicyException resources, Gatekeeper constraint exclusions, Falco rule exceptionsA risk owner with authority over the serviceWhich events are retained, for how long, and who reads them?Kubernetes audit policy levels and the log backend’s retentionSecurity operations and platform A note on naming: Pod Security Standards define a profile called baseline. That profile is one useful input, but the baseline in this post is the wider organisational agreement that includes it. Looking at the table, no single team owns every row. A platform team that deploys all of these tools alone has implemented the mechanisms and guessed at the intent. That is the new silo in its most concrete form. Make the baseline cheap to ask about The answer is not to send platform teams back to a security approval queue. It is to make the cross-team parts of the baseline easy to reach. Treating the baseline as code is a practical way to do that, because it uses workflows engineering teams already know: Keep policies in a repository, alongside the admission policies, Falco rules and audit policy that implement them. Make ownership explicit with code owners. A CODEOWNERS file can require review from security for the paths that define block-or-report decisions, and from application teams for the runtime rules that describe their workloads. Ownership stops being implicit knowledge. Turn exceptions into pull requests. Each exception records the policy it bypasses, the workload it applies to, who approved it and when it expires. Expiry needs enforcement too, such as a scheduled CI check that fails when an exception has passed its date. An exception with no expiry is a permanent policy change nobody reviewed. Start in report mode on purpose. Running new policies in Audit or warn first is a good practice, as long as there is an agreed date and owner for the move to enforcement. Otherwise report mode becomes the permanent state. Publish a clear contact and response expectation for each owning team. A code owner who takes three weeks to review is an approval queue with better tooling. Security teams carry half of this. When guidance is hard to find or exceptions are slow, teams have every incentive to work around the process. Autonomy is not the problem. Expensive help is. Four decisions that rarely belong to the same person Once a team acts, four decisions have to be made explicit: DecisionWho should hold itHow it usually failsDefine the expected outcomeSecurity, risk or architectureA policy statement nobody can testImplement and operate itThe team that owns the platform or serviceSecurity ends up doing it, or it is done once and never maintainedAccept the residual riskA role with authority over the service and the budget to remediateWhoever understands the technical detail, or security by defaultVerify it stays effectiveSecurity or another independent functionImplementation is treated as proof, and drift goes unnoticed The third row is where most programmes quietly break. The person who approves an exception must be able to fund its remediation or carry the consequence if it never happens. Someone who can sign but cannot fund is not accepting a risk. They are witnessing it. Frameworks describe the same split. In NIST CSF 2.0, GV.RR-02 asks for roles, responsibilities and authorities to be established, communicated, understood and enforced. GV.RR-03 expects resources to match the risk strategy, and ID.RA-07 asks for exceptions to be assessed, recorded and tracked. In the EU, NIS2 Article 20 and DORA Article 5 place accountability on the management body rather than on a security team. None of these require a team to go it alone. They require that authority, funding and the exception path are explicit. Takeaway A silo is not a team that stopped asking permission. It is a team that stopped asking for help. Deploying a runtime security tool, an admission controller or an audit pipeline is the easy part, and a platform team can do it independently. Defining what those tools should enforce is a cross-team decision, and pretending otherwise is how the new silo forms. A simple habit at kick-off: for each row of the baseline, ask who owns the answer, when it is needed and how to reach them. When work stalls, ask what made going alone seem like the best option before assigning blame. Was guidance easy to find? Could the right people respond in time? Was the exception path clear? Autonomy works best when a team can act, knows where the rest of the answer lives and can reach the people who have it without friction. Trust and collaboration are not the opposite of ownership. They are what make it sustainable. References Kubernetes, Pod Security Standards and Auditing Falco documentation Kyverno documentation OPA Gatekeeper documentation Sigstore documentation NIST Cybersecurity Framework 2.0 (CSWP 29): GV.RR-02, GV.RR-03, ID.RA-07 Directive (EU) 2022/2555 (NIS2), Article 20 Regulation (EU) 2022/2554 (DORA), Article 5 This post describes an engineering operating model, not a legal interpretation or a universal assignment of responsibilities. Adapt it to your organization’s structure and risk management process.

title: [Cloudflare] How Cloudflare WAF protects against ruby2shell (CVE-2026-132825)
summary: On November 19, 2026, the Ruby team disclosed ruby2shell (CVE-2026-132825), a heap buffer overflow in the way Ruby changes the case of strings. Ruby rates the flaw Critical and says it is aware of proofs of concept that achieve remote code execution in some scenarios. Fixes shipped in Ruby 3.3.14, 3.4.13, and 4.0.10.The reach is wide. Veria Labs reports that Ruby on Rails and classic-style Sinatra applications reach the bug in their default configuration, before any authentication. Self-hosted products that bundle Ruby, including GitLab, GitHub Enterprise Server, Mastodon, OpenProject, Discourse and Chatwoot, shipped an affected Ruby in their latest release at the time of disclosure.Cloudflare WAF blocks ruby2shell for all customers, including those on the Free plan. We have added two rules to both the Cloudflare Free Managed Ruleset and the Cloudflare Managed Ruleset, with Block as the default action: one for ruby2shell and one for GHSA-87fm-7w84-j2px, a related integer overflow in Ruby string case conversion fixed in the same releases.The WAF is a compensating control, not a replacement for patching. Exploits can reach the bug through paths a WAF does not see, and the only complete fix is to upgrade Ruby. Our team continues to monitor attack traffic and will update the rules as new techniques appear. You can track rule changes in the WAF changelog and get the latest on the vulnerability in the Cloudflare Zero Wire briefing.Cloudflare has patched its own systems that use Ruby, and we have found no indication of compromise.What we know about ruby2shellRuby strings carry an encoding, and Ruby still supports many legacy single-byte encodings, such as ISO-8859-1 (Latin-1) and Windows-1252, alongside UTF-8. In a single-byte encoding each character takes one byte, so changing the case of a string usually produces output of the same length.The German sharp s (ß) breaks that assumption. Its uppercase form is two characters, SS. In 14 ISO-8859 and Windows-125x encodings, Ruby writes those two bytes but checks for room for only one. According to Veria Labs, a string with 21 sharp s characters overflows the output buffer by one byte. The methods that reach the bug are upcase, swapcase, downcase(:fold) and casecmp?. UTF-8 strings take a different code path and are not affected.A one-byte overflow can look harmless. In a memory-corruption exploit, though, a single byte written past the end of a heap buffer can be enough to corrupt an adjacent object or allocator metadata. Ruby says it is aware of proofs of concept that turn this flaw into code execution, and Veria Labs says it will publish its own proof of concept about a week after disclosure. We expect scanning to start soon after.Why default Rails and Sinatra apps are exposedHTML forms can only send GET and POST requests. To simulate PUT, PATCH, or DELETE, many web frameworks accept a _method parameter in a POST request. Rack, the interface most Ruby web frameworks build on, implements this in its MethodOverride middleware, which converts the value of _method to uppercase. Rails includes this middleware by default, and classic-style Sinatra applications enable it. An attacker can send a multipart POST request whose _method part declares a legacy character set and contains a run of sharp s characters. The framework upcases the value while it is still routing the request, before any application code or authentication check runs.Veria Labs reports that other frameworks and plain Rack applications are not exposed by default. Application code that changes the case of strings received in a legacy encoding may still be affected, wherever the string comes from.Who is affectedConditionDetailsRuby versionRuby 3.3.13 and earlier, 3.4.0 through 3.4.12, and 4.0.0 through 4.0.9. Veria Labs reports the bug has been present since Ruby 2.4.0. Ruby 3.2 and earlier have reached end of life and will not receive the fix.FrameworkRails and classic-style Sinatra in their default configuration. Any other code that changes the case of attacker-controlled strings in a legacy single-byte encoding.Bundled softwareAs of November 19, 2026, Veria Labs lists GitLab 19.6.0, GitHub Enterprise Server 3.22.5, Mastodon 4.7.5, OpenProject 17.9.7, Discourse 2026.10.1 and Chatwoot 4.20.0 as bundling an affected Ruby in their latest release. Discourse moved its Docker base image to Ruby 4.0.10 on November 19, so rebuilding a Docker install picks up the fix.Distribution packages can backport fixes without changing the Ruby version number, so check the full package version against your distribution's advisory.Six more Ruby flaws in the same releaseRuby 3.3.14, 3.4.13, and 4.0.10 also fix six other memory safety flaws, and Ruby says several of them can lead to code execution. One, GHSA-87fm-7w84-j2px, is an integer overflow in the same string case conversion code, and our second WAF rule covers it. The other five are in Ruby's regular expression engine. Most of them require the application to compile or match a regular expression pattern supplied by the attacker. That is uncommon in web applications, but it does happen in search features, filtering rules and admin tools.How Cloudflare WAF protects youUpgrading every Ruby runtime takes time, especially when Ruby is bundled inside self-hosted products and container images. Cloudflare WAF reduces your exposure while you patch.New managed rules, on for every customerBoth rules are part of the Cloudflare Free Managed Ruleset and the Cloudflare Managed Ruleset (Ruleset ID efb7b8c949ac4650a09736fc376e9aee), with Block as the default action.Rule descriptionRule IDRulesetDefault actionRuby - Heap Overflow - CVE:CVE-2026-1328257328f23691e44b07892ebd25b19210f1Cloudflare Free Managed Ruleset (Free plan)BlockRuby - Heap Overflow - CVE:CVE-2026-1328251afa543a1ed84893b01df04c34402c88Cloudflare Managed Ruleset (Pro, Business and Enterprise plans)BlockRuby - Integer Overflow - GHSA-87fm-7w84-j2px8660e37e86444f9f9267ba22e9855f05Cloudflare Free Managed Ruleset (Free plan)BlockRuby - Integer Overflow - GHSA-87fm-7w84-j2px6defac6a52334542adf4a162daf25922Cloudflare Managed Ruleset (Pro, Business and Enterprise plans)BlockOn the Free plan, the Cloudflare Free Managed Ruleset runs automatically, so there is nothing to turn on. On paid plans, the rules are active wherever the Cloudflare Managed Ruleset is deployed. Because paid plans give you more control over how rulesets are deployed, the Cloudflare Managed Ruleset may not be active on every zone. We recommend checking its status to confirm that it is running. You can use the links in the Zero Wire briefing to go straight to the rules in your dashboard.What the WAF cannot seeA WAF can block an exploit when the malicious input arrives in an HTTP request that passes through Cloudflare. It cannot block every path to the vulnerable code:Traffic that bypasses Cloudflare. Requests sent directly to your origin IP address, and traffic between internal services, never reach the WAF. Configure your origin to accept traffic only from Cloudflare, for example with Cloudflare Tunnel or Authenticated Origin Pulls.Other entry points into the same code. Ruby code that changes the case of strings from email, file imports, message queues or background jobs can reach ruby2shell without an HTTP request.Adding defense in depth with WAF attack scoreMemory corruption is usually only the first step. To run commands, an attacker still has to deliver a second-stage payload, such as shell commands or a reverse shell, and then interact with the compromised server. WAF attack score uses machine learning to score each request for remote code execution payloads, which helps catch exploit variations and post-exploitation traffic that signature-based rules can miss. Create a custom rule that blocks or challenges requests with cf.waf.score.rce le 20 on Enterprise plans, or cf.waf.score.class eq "attack" on Business plans.Impact on Cloudflare infrastructureCloudflare has patched its systems that use Ruby against ruby2shell. We have found no indication of compromise and continue to monitor.Patch nowruby2shell turns a one-byte miscalculation in string case conversion into a pre-authentication path to code execution in default Rails and Sinatra apps. With a public proof of concept expected within days, the window to patch is short. Here is what to do:Check your WAF coverage. On the Free plan, the ruby2shell rules are already blocking. On paid plans, confirm the Cloudflare Managed Ruleset is deployed and the rules have not been overridden.Upgrade Ruby to 3.3.14, 3.4.13 or 4.0.10 and restart every Ruby process, including background workers. Rebuild container images. Move applications on Ruby 3.2 or earlier to a supported series.Update self-hosted products that bundle Ruby, such as GitLab, GitHub Enterprise Server, Mastodon, OpenProject and Chatwoot, as each vendor releases a fix. Rebuild Discourse Docker installs now.Inventory your runtimes. The Zero Wire briefing includes a prompt you can give an AI agent to find every affected Ruby runtime in your infrastructure.Our WAF analysts will keep updating protections as new techniques appear. Follow the WAF changelog for rule updates.

title: [Cloudflare] How Cloudflare WAF helps protect against phpAfterShell and other critical PHP flaws
summary: On November 19, 2026, the security research company depthfirst disclosed phpAfterShell (CVE-2026-126714), a vulnerability in PHP's default file-based session handler that can lead to remote code execution. Under the Common Vulnerability Scoring System (CVSS) 4.0, it scores 9.2 out of 10 (Critical). The PHP project fixed it the same day in versions 8.2.36, 8.3.37, 8.4.28, 8.5.13, and 8.6.0. These releases fix 16 other security vulnerabilities, six of them also rated critical.Cloudflare’s web application firewall (WAF) blocks known phpAfterShell attack patterns, including for customers on the Free plan. The protection comes from a PHP remote code execution rule we first deployed in October 2026 for the php2shell vulnerabilities. That rule already detected part of the phpAfterShell attack pattern before the vulnerability was disclosed, and on November 19 we updated its detection logic to cover phpAfterShell. The rule is part of both the Cloudflare Free Managed Ruleset and the Cloudflare Managed Ruleset, is enabled by default, and its default action is Block.In the same WAF release, we added three new rules to the Cloudflare Managed Ruleset for paid plans: one for a request smuggling flaw in PHP-FPM (CVE-2026-129289), and two for flaws in PHP's SOAP extension (CVE-2026-15353 and CVE-2026-129506) that PHP fixed in the same releases. These rules are enabled by default with the Log action, because the request patterns they look for can also appear in legitimate traffic, and blocking by default could disrupt it. Customers can review matching requests in Security Events now and change the action to Block once they confirm the rules do not affect legitimate traffic.The WAF is an additional layer of defense, not a replacement for the patch. Several of the critical flaws depend on server configuration or can be reached through paths a WAF does not see, and the only complete fix is to upgrade PHP and restart every worker. Our analysts continue to monitor attack activity and will update the rules as new techniques and variations appear. You can track rule changes in the WAF changelog and follow how the vulnerabilities develop in the dedicated Cloudflare Zero Wire briefing.There appears to be no indication so far that these vulnerabilities have been exploited. As of November 19, 2026, none of the 17 vulnerabilities was listed in CISA's Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog, and no source we reviewed reports exploitation in the wild.What we know about phpAfterShellPHP stores session data in files by default. When an application calls session_start(), PHP reads the session file and deserializes its content into the $_SESSION array. When the request ends, PHP writes the updated session back to the same file.phpAfterShell is triggered when that write is interrupted. The session file can then hold the beginning of the new session data followed by the end of the old one. On the next request, session_start() deserializes this mixed content. If an attacker controlled the old data, PHP can end up deserializing objects of the attacker's choice.An attacker trying to exploit the flaw is likely to first search for a way to place controlled data in the session. PHP's advisory names two:Session upload progress, a PHP feature that writes information about a running file upload into the session. A remote client can use it to shape the stored data.Applications that store large user-controlled strings in the session.According to PHP, code execution also requires an interruption at a useful point in the write and a suitable deserialization gadget chain in the application. depthfirst reports that it reached code execution without an application gadget by chaining a second, undisclosed memory-corruption bug in a PHP-native class. The sources we reviewed do not establish whether that second bug is fixed in the November 19 releases.depthfirst says it discovered and reported phpAfterShell. The CVE record credits Leo Lin and Asahi as reporters.The other critical flawsThe same releases fix six more critical vulnerabilities. Each one needs a specific configuration to be exploitable:CVEComponentImpactConditionsCVE-2026-129289PHP-FPMAn unauthenticated attacker can smuggle a second FastCGI request into PHP-FPM and run PHP code as the worker.A front end that reuses backend FastCGI connections (nginx with fastcgi_keep_conn on, Apache mod_proxy_fcgi with enablereuse=on, or HAProxy), an application path that opens php://input without reading it to the end, and the path of an existing PHP script.CVE-2026-115560Session serializerObject injection through a mismatch between session serializers. First covered in our php2shell briefing, now fixed.Session upload progress enabled. PHP widened the scope: applications, pools or command-line jobs that use different serializers and share a session store are affected.CVE-2026-129496Timezone cacheUse-after-free that can crash a fresh worker and possibly run code. PHP demonstrated code execution locally with known memory addresses.Non-thread-safe builds where a startup diagnostic has been written to a PHP error log file.CVE-2026-129481Session shutdownUse-after-free, described by PHP as an incomplete fix for CVE-2026-109619. No code execution demonstrated.PHP 8.3 and later.CVE-2026-129474Fatal error backtracesUse-after-free in magic method backtraces.PHP 8.5 and later, where fatal error backtraces are enabled by default. Setting zend.exception_ignore_args=1, the php.ini-production default, blocks the demonstrated attack.CVE-2026-129182Fatal error backtracesUse-after-free. No code execution demonstrated.PHP 8.5, specific path-level settings, and an Apache per-directory configuration or front end that produces an early diagnostic.Who is affectedThe vulnerable versions are PHP 8.2 before 8.2.36, 8.3 before 8.3.37, 8.4 before 8.4.28, 8.5 before 8.5.13, and the 8.6.0 release candidates. Whether a deployment is exposed depends on the conditions of each flaw.PHP 8.1 and earlier are end-of-life. depthfirst says the official 7.4, 8.0 and 8.1 end-of-life mitigation branches are not affected by phpAfterShell, but PHP says CVE-2026-129289 was introduced in PHP 5.6.0 and that releases older than 8.2 may also be affected by CVE-2026-115560.Linux distributions often backport fixes without changing the PHP version number. Check the full package version against your distribution's advisory.How Cloudflare WAF protects youPHP runs a large share of the web, often inside content management systems, plugins, and container images that teams do not update directly. It cannot block every path to these vulnerabilities, including:The deserialization step. phpAfterShell's final step happens inside PHP, when it reads a corrupted session file. The WAF can block the requests that plant the payload, not the read itself.Session data from other sources. If an application copies user-controlled data into the session from a database, a queue or an upstream API, that data may never cross the WAF in a recognizable form.Flaws triggered by server state. CVE-2026-129496, CVE-2026-129481, CVE-2026-129474 and CVE-2026-129182 depend on error logs, diagnostics and worker lifecycle. They do not have dedicated WAF rules, and the patch and the configuration changes below are the way to address them.Traffic that bypasses Cloudflare. This includes internal traffic between services and PHP-FPM listeners exposed directly to a network.Adding defense in depth with WAF attack scoreWAF attack score adds a machine learning layer that scores each request for attack payloads. It is available on Business plans (cf.waf.score.class) and, with a dedicated remote code execution sub-score (cf.waf.score.rce) along with an overall score (cf.waf.score), on Enterprise plans.Attack score complements the managed rules. It will not recognize every serialized object or smuggled FastCGI record on its own, but a working exploit chain usually needs more than one request, and the later stages carry payloads the model is trained to score:Second-stage payloads. Once an attacker can run code, they still need to send commands: shell execution primitives (/bin/sh -c, system(), passthru()), PHP code evaluation (eval(), assert()) or reverse-shell strings in headers, query parameters or request bodies.Webshell traffic. Attackers often drop a small PHP webshell after the initial compromise. Requests that pass operating system commands to that webshell remain visible to attack score.Deploy protections and patchYou can find more information on how to deploy managed rules and attack score in our WAF guide. In short:Check that phpAfterShell protection is active. On the Free plan, no action is needed. The CVE-2026-129289, CVE-2026-15353 and CVE-2026-129506 rules are in Log mode by default. Review their matches in Security Events, then change their action to Block.Layer attack score. Create a custom rule that blocks or challenges requests with a low remote code execution score, for example cf.waf.score.rce le 20 on Enterprise plans, or cf.waf.score.class eq "attack" on Business plans.Upgrade PHP. Move to 8.2.36, 8.3.37, 8.4.28, 8.5.13 or 8.6.0. Rebuild container images and restart the PHP-FPM master or Apache so every worker loads the new binary, then verify the version that serves web requests. After upgrading, check that no php.ini, FPM pool or virtual host still sets session.upload_progress.enabled=1, because an explicit setting overrides the new default.Apply interim mitigations if you cannot upgrade right away. Set session.upload_progress.enabled=0 and limit the untrusted data you store in sessions. Turn off FastCGI connection reuse. On PHP 8.5, set fatal_error_backtraces=0. Fix configuration errors that produce PHP startup warnings, or send PHP errors to syslog instead of a file. Keep PHP-FPM listeners off untrusted networks. These steps reduce exposure; they do not fix the flaws.For a prompt you can give an AI agent to inventory your PHP deployments and check each one against all seven critical CVEs, see the phpAfterShell page on Cloudflare Zero Wire.Update every PHP runtime nowphpAfterShell turns an interrupted file write in PHP's default session handler into a path to code execution, and it arrived in the same release as six other critical flaws. With technical details now public, we expect exploit attempts to follow. Cloudflare WAF blocks known phpAfterShell attack patterns for every customer, including the Free plan, and paid plans have new rules for the PHP-FPM and SOAP flaws. The fix is still to upgrade PHP and restart the services that use it.

title: [Pulumi] Trigger Pulumi Agents from Infrastructure Events
summary: Pulumi Agents can start work automatically in response to a Pulumi event or a webhook. With a trigger, you can give an agent a recurring assignment and choose when it should start. For events in Pulumi Cloud, that choice can be as specific as a failed update on a single stack. A failed deployment is one use for a trigger. The agent can read the failed update, identify the affected resource, and post a diagnosis in Slack. That puts the error and a suggested next step in the deployment channel for the team to review. A trigger for failed deployments The example below defines an agent and a trigger in TypeScript. The trigger selects failed updates on checkout/prod and starts an investigation. The agent has read access to the stack’s update history and instructions to report what failed and what to check next. The agent’s instructions describe what you want to learn from each failure. Its roleId determines what it can read. Here, agentRoleId is a configuration key that holds the ID of an existing Pulumi Cloud role with stack:read on checkout/prod. The configuration steps below show how to look up that ID and supply it through Pulumi ESC. import * as pulumi from "@pulumi/pulumi"; import * as service from "@pulumi/pulumiservice"; const config = new pulumi.Config(); const orgName = pulumi.getOrganization(); const agent = new service.api.agents.Definition("troubleshooter", { orgName, name: "deployment-troubleshooter", displayName: "Deployment Troubleshooter", roleId: config.require("agentRoleId"), customInstructions: .join(" "), }); Start a task when an update fails Add the automation to the same program. Its trigger matches three details that Pulumi Cloud records for a stack operation: the stack, the operation, and the result. When an update to checkout/prod finishes with a failed result, Pulumi starts a task for the agent referenced by agent.definitionID. new service.api.AgentAutomationV2("failed-update", { orgName, name: "Investigate failed production updates", kind: "triggered", trigger: { type: "stack_operation", stacks: , operations: , results: , quietPeriodSeconds: 30, }, task: { agentDefinitionId: agent.definitionID, toolExecutionMode: "cloud", message: { type: "user_message", content: "Investigate this failed update." }, }, notificationTargets: , }); The first failure starts the task immediately. The 30-second window lets subsequent matching events join the investigation. The agent reads the update using its Pulumi Cloud role, and Pulumi delivers the findings to the Slack channel in notificationTargets. Configure and deploy Create a TypeScript project named deployment-agents with pulumi new typescript --name deployment-agents, and put both code snippets above in its index.ts. Select a stack for that project in the same Pulumi Cloud organization as checkout/prod. Find the role ID. With a Pulumi account that can list roles in your organization, run the command below. Replace YOUR_ORG with the organization name. The output lists each role’s name and ID. Copy the ID of the role you’ve granted read access to checkout/prod. pulumi api /api/orgs/YOUR_ORG/roles --method GET -F uxPurpose=role | jq -r '.roles |  | @tsv' Connect the Slack channel. Have a workspace admin install the Pulumi Slack app. In Pulumi Cloud, link the account you’ll use to deploy the automation to your Slack identity under Account settings > Pulumi Agents. This lets Pulumi find channels in your workspace. Invite the app to your deployment channel and copy the channel ID from its details in Slack. Supply both IDs through ESC. Add the following to an ESC environment named deployment-agents/settings. The deployment-agents prefix on each key matches the project name in Pulumi.yaml. values: pulumiConfig: deployment-agents:agentRoleId: "<Pulumi Cloud role ID>" deployment-agents:slackChannelId: "<Slack channel ID>" From the deployment-agents project, import the environment into the selected stack and deploy: npm install @pulumi/pulumiservice@1.7.0 pulumi config env add deployment-agents/settings pulumi up pulumi up creates the Deployment Troubleshooter agent and the Investigate failed production updates automation. The automation begins watching checkout/prod. What the team sees in Slack In a live test on a disposable stack, the check-release-manifest resource ran a local command to verify that release-manifest.json existed. The file was absent, so the update failed. Pulumi posted the automation’s name in the deployment channel as soon as the investigation started. The agent then replied in the Slack thread with its diagnosis. check-release-manifest had failed with Missing release-manifest.json. The agent suggested checking whether the build had generated the file and whether the command was looking in the right directory. Selecting Continue in Pulumi opened the full investigation for that update.

title: [Microsoft Azure] Predicting and detecting failures: How Azure strengthens reliability for mission-critical workloads
summary: Takeaway: Azure Failure Prediction and Detection (AFPD) is Microsoft Azure’s end-to-end system aiming to catch hardware failures before they interrupt a workload, not after. Across the Azure fleet, AFPD has improved the prevention of hardware-related VM interruptions by 36%. SAP workloads offer a compelling example of AFPD’s value, illustrating why preventing interruptions matters for mission-critical services. But AFPD isn’t specific to SAP: it operates across General Purpose, Specialized Compute, HPC/AI, and select Storage workloads, making SAP’s experience a window into Azure’s broader approach to reliability for mission-critical third-party services. To learn more, watch our companion video to learn how AFPD helps reduce the risk of failures disrupting your critical workloads. Reliability engineered into the platform Most conversations about cloud reliability focus on what you build: zone-redundant architectures, failover patterns, and backup strategies. Less visible, but just as consequential, is what the platform does on your behalf; before a failure ever becomes an incident you need to respond to. That’s the premise behind AFPD, which became fully operational in 2024. AFPD is an end-to-end system that uses machine learning and telemetry to predict, mitigate, and remediate hardware failures in the Azure fleet before they interrupt your workloads. For a deep dive discussion into this capability, see the companion post here. How does AFPD predict and prevent hardware failures? Historically, hardware failures on any cloud platform follow a familiar pattern: a component degrades, your workload is interrupted, an engineer investigates, and a reboot or hardware replacement follows. This is the old model Azure has spent years moving away from, one built around mission-critical escalations, supply chain constraints, and manual recovery. AFPD replaces that pattern with three coordinated phases: Predict and detect: Machine learning models and detection rules continuously monitor telemetry across the Azure fleet, node behavior, component signals, and hardware-specific indicators like Solid State Drive (SSD) health, to catch patterns that indicate an active or likely future failure. Mitigate: Once a node is flagged, the mitigation service marks it not allocatable for new workloads and, where eligible, live-migrates existing customer workloads to a healthy node with no reboot, typically just a pause of a few seconds. Live migration is available on many, but not all M-series sized virtual machines (VMs); check the feature support table for more information. Where live migration isn’t possible, a notification with a redeploy deadline and recommended action is posted to the VMs Resource Health and Scheduled Events. Remediate: The affected node is pulled from production, tagged with diagnostic detail so technicians can skip redundant troubleshooting, repaired using proactively staged spare parts, and returned to the fleet. In practice, this coordinated approach has delivered measurable gains: AFPD has increased the monthly node repair rate by 80%. The result is a system that doesn’t just react faster; in many cases, it prevents the interruption from reaching you. This approach has reduced the overall number of hardware reboots by more than 36%, and the underlying system won the Best Paper Award at the 2025 IEEE Cloud Summit for its approach to predicting, mitigating, and remediating node interruptions at scale. What SAP’s result means for other workloads Every customer benefits from fewer interruptions, but SAP workloads make the case for AFPD unusually clear. SAP systems are highly sensitive to downtime; they are often the system of record for finance, supply chain, and operations, and even brief interruptions carry outsized business impact. A platform that has the ability to predict or detect hardware issues and reduce their impact before you experience an interruption isn’t a convenience for SAP customers; it’s foundational to running SAP on Azure with confidence. That sensitivity also exposed a real gap the team was candid about: many SAP customers aren’t yet aware of the notification and automation options available to them. AFPD surfaces its findings through four consistent, customer-facing channels: Resource Health, for viewing detailed health events and recommended actions on individual VMs, including live migration eligibility and redeployment deadlines. Resource Graph Explorer, for querying health status across your fleet, including large SAP landscapes that require programmatic visibility. Event Grid, for wiring AFPD events directly into your own monitoring and automation, with Azure Functions, webhooks, or REST APIs. Scheduled Events, for receiving advance VM event notifications through IMDS, enabling configured SAP HA clusters to move resources off affected nodes. The notification content is identical across Resource Health, Resource Graph, and Event Grid, so the channel you choose is a matter of scale and integration preference, not information quality. For SAP customers running at scale, that consistency is what makes automated, hands-off resiliency actually practical. It’s tempting to read AFPD as an SAP-specific feature. It isn’t. SAP is simply where the stakes are high enough that the system’s value becomes obvious fastest. AFPD operates across Azure Compute’s General Purpose and Specialized Compute offerings, HPC/AI workloads, and select Storage scenarios, meaning the same predictive, self-healing infrastructure protecting SAP landscapes today is the same infrastructure underpinning every mission-critical third-party service hosted on Azure. That’s the broader narrative worth taking away: AFPD isn’t a tier you pay up for or something you have to configure at the infrastructure layer; it runs automatically across the fleet. It’s an active, continuously improving discipline, one where machine learning models get better at predicting failure over time, where remediation gets faster because spares are already staged, and where your first signal of a problem is often a notification that it’s already been handled. For any ISV or enterprise running a downtime intolerant workload on Azure, SAP’s experience with AFPD is a preview, not an exception. What to do next Check your own notification setup. If you’re running SAP or another mission-critical workload on Azure, confirm you’re consuming AFPD events through one of these: Resource Health (RHC): Best for looking at the health of one VM, including what happened and why. Resource Graph (ARG): Best for finding affected VMs at scale across many subscriptions in a single query. Event Grid: Best for automation, since it pushes notifications as health changes so you can react without polling. Events can be sent to a REST webhook endpoint or an Azure Functions, and onward to other services such as Logic Apps, Event Hubs, or Azure Monitor alerts. Prepare your automation for Scheduled Events: Make sure your automation can process Scheduled Events for Azure Virtual Machines, including events with a NotBefore time up to seven days in the future. Configure Pacemaker for Azure Scheduled Events: For SAP high-availability clusters, follow the guidance for configuring the Pacemaker azure-events-az resource agent leveraging the relevant guides for SUSE Linux Enterprise Server (SLES) in Azure or RHEL in Azure. Watch the full conversation. The SAP on Azure podcast episode goes deeper into the live demo of Resource Health, Resource Graph, and Event Grid notifications than this post can cover. Go deeper technically. The IEEE paper, AFPD: System for Prediction, Mitigation and Remediation of Node Interruptions in Cloud Infrastructure (IEEE) (2025 IEEE Cloud Summit Best Paper), covers the ML models and system architecture in full detail. title: [Microsoft Azure] The Platform Behind the Next AI Breakthrough
summary: This article has been written and paid for by Microsoft. The content is not WIRED editorial content. The content does not necessarily reflect the views of WIRED, its affiliates, or owner, and does not reflect any endorsement direct or indirect of Microsoft, its affiliates, or other clients. The next frontier of AI is coming into focus as agents take on longer, more strategic work. They can write and validate code, coordinate across systems, rebalance inventory as conditions change, manage production operations, or carry a migration from plan to completion. AI is no longer supporting one step; it is executing and reshaping the process itself. New models help drive this change by expanding what AI can reason about, create, and accomplish. But the combination of advances in models and infrastructure is key to moving agents from isolated tasks to sustained, high-impact work. Realizing that potential requires silicon, compute, storage, and networking to work together so workloads run faster and more reliably at scale. Agents Are a Different Kind of Workload Cloud infrastructure has evolved before to support new kinds of applications. Even the most advanced cloud-native applications often followed predictable request-and-response paths. To deliver this at scale, cloud-native architectures turned to containers, distributed services, and dynamic scaling, to make the platform more automated and flexible. Agentic applications build on that foundation but introduce another shift: long-running work whose path and resource needs are dynamic and often unpredictable. An agent may work for hours or days, moving between reasoning, data retrieval, tool use, and code execution while preserving progress between steps. Its needs may shift throughout the task. It might require a burst of computing power for one step, fast access to large amounts of data for another, and then pause while another tool or another agent finishes its work. Supporting this ebb and flow requires the platform to evolve again—this time around how agents operate. Infrastructure Must Work as One System Every layer of infrastructure is evolving for AI. Compute must respond to the changing demand of agentic workloads. Storage must preserve progress across long-running work. And networking must move data quickly among models, tools, and business systems. But improving each layer independently is no longer enough. Agent performance depends on how well those layers are evolving and how well they all work together. More computing power will not help if the platform cannot move data quickly or maintain progress between steps. Silicon, compute, storage, and networking need to be co-designed and continuously optimized as one system. This integrated approach also changes infrastructure operations. Teams need a complete view of performance, capacity, and cost so they can find bottlenecks and improve the full workload instead of tuning one component at a time. That system-wide view helps turn infrastructure improvements into faster, more reliable, cost-effective workloads. Different Workloads, One Operational Approach That consistent operational view becomes even more important as teams choose different technologies for different workloads. A customer-facing agent may prioritize low latency, while a complex workflow may need deeper reasoning. Teams need the freedom to choose the right model, run time, silicon, and environment for each workload while balancing performance and cost. But more choice can create operational complexity because each combination may require a different approach to deployment, monitoring, and optimization. An integrated platform preserves flexibility while giving teams a consistent way to operate across models and infrastructure. Teams can choose what works best without managing every combination differently. Levi Strauss & Co. And the Value of an Integrated Platform Levi Strauss & Co. began its path to AI transformation by preparing existing business systems for the future. The company moved its data centers to Microsoft Azure, consolidated ERP platforms, modernized applications, and unified its data in a governed, real-time layer. But that was only the beginning. Levi Strauss & Co. is now building a unified “super agent” to coordinate more than 1,000 domain-specific agents. Its platform must support both the critical processes that run the business today and a new class of intelligent workloads that coordinates work across functions. The lesson is clear: A durable platform must be built for current applications and whatever AI makes possible next. Three practical tests for an agentic platform Technical leaders can begin with three questions to assess readiness for an agentic platform. First, do I have the high-performance compute, storage, and networking that models and agents need—or am I trying to run tomorrow’s applications on yesterday’s platform? Second, can I choose the right model, run time, silicon, and location for each agentic workload while balancing performance, cost, complexity, and risk? Third, can I use agents to operate the platform by moving workloads into production faster, resolving incidents before disruption, and continuously improving performance, reliability, and AI economics? Building for the next decade The next decade of AI will not be defined by a single breakthrough. Models will become even more capable, agents will take on work we have not yet imagined, and infrastructure demands will shift with them. Organizations need a durable platform that can embrace each new wave of innovation without being rebuilt whenever the frontier moves. Azure is the platform foundation for that future. Microsoft has spent years bringing some of the world’s most advanced and demanding AI solutions online at massive scale. The lessons from that work continually shape Azure silicon, compute, storage, networking, and operations—and make those capabilities available to customers. This is the opportunity of Frontier Transformation: continually turning advances across the AI stack into new ways to operate, compete, and grow. Learn more at azure.com. The post The Platform Behind the Next AI Breakthrough appeared first on Microsoft Azure Blog.

title: [Docker] The Trust Layer: Securing Agentic AI with Docker AI Governance
summary: The Agent Trust Gap The security problem changes once an AI agent can do more than answer a prompt. It can execute code, access files, connect to services, and call external tools. That creates a new security question for enterprises: how do you give an agent enough freedom to be useful without giving it more access than it actually needs? A model decision is not automatically an authorized action. That distinction becomes important the moment an agent can turn a model output into an action in a real system. The answer can’t rely only on the model. Agent behavior can vary, while security controls need to be clear and enforceable. That means putting controls around the environment where the agent runs, what it can access, which tools it can use, and what happens when a policy allows or blocks an action. For a CISO, this creates a trust gap. Approving the use of AI agents means being able to answer more than whether the model is capable: what access does the agent have, where are those boundaries enforced, and what evidence is available afterward? The goal is to let teams adopt agents without making model behavior itself the security boundary. Docker AI Governance approaches this through three areas: Sandbox Policies, MCP Tool Governance, and Audit + Visibility. Together, they address three practical questions security teams need answered: Where can the agent operate? What can it do? And can we see what happened? In this article, I use “trust layer” as shorthand for the infrastructure between what an agent wants to do and what the organization actually allows it to do. There is a related trust question too: what software artifacts are these agentic workflows building and using? Docker Hardened Images address that software supply-chain side of the problem, alongside the runtime controls discussed below. Figure 1: The three layers of Docker AI Governance: Sandbox Policies, MCP Tool Governance, and Audit + Visibility. Sandbox Policies: Where Can the Agent Operate? An agent needs enough access to get real work done. A coding agent may need to install packages, build containers, edit project files, or connect to external services. The security challenge is deciding where those actions are allowed before the agent starts taking them. Docker Sandboxes give each agent an isolated microVM environment a lightweight virtual machine with its own Docker Engine, filesystem, and network. Docker AI Governance adds policy around that environment so security teams can control network and filesystem access centrally. Network policies can allow or block specific domains, IP ranges, and ports. Filesystem policies control which host paths can be mounted into a sandbox and whether that access is read-only or read-write. These controls are enforced at the network proxy and filesystem mount layers rather than depending on the agent to follow an instruction. For an organization, that means the same boundaries can follow developers across their sandboxes instead of being configured differently on every machine. Teams still get the access they need for their work, but an individual agent cannot simply expand those boundaries on its own. A developer can check the effective boundary before starting the agent: $ sbx policy check network api.anthropic.com Allowed: api.anthropic.com $ sbx policy check network blocked.example.com Denied: blocked.example.com The important part is that the result comes from the active policy, not from an instruction the agent is expected to follow. This answers the first governance question: Where can the agent operate? MCP Tool Governance: What Can the Agent Do? Once an agent has a controlled place to run, the next question is what it should be allowed to do through external tools. MCP (Model Context Protocol) gives agents a common way to connect to external tools, services, and capabilities, but that also expands what an agent can act on. For enterprise use, making a tool available should not automatically mean every agent can use it. Docker AI Governance puts policy around MCP activity handled through Docker’s MCP Gateway. Administrators can control which MCP servers may be registered and what agents can do through them, including tool calls, resources, prompts, and approval requirements. These organization policies are written in Cedar, a policy language used to express authorization rules. When MCP policy enforcement is active, governed requests are denied unless a matching policy permits them. For example, a policy can permit read-only tool calls for a specific registered MCP server: permit (principal, action == MCP::Action::"invokeTool", resource) when { resource in MCP::Server::"example" && resource.readOnly == true }; Here, readOnly comes from the MCP tool’s annotations. Those annotations are supplied by the server and are advisory, so this example relies on metadata provided by that server. This makes tool access an explicit policy decision rather than something left to each agent or developer to configure independently. A team can be given access to the tools it needs, while other servers or actions remain unavailable. Policies can also require confirmation for specific tool calls when an action needs an additional checkpoint. One boundary is worth making clear: MCP policies apply to activity handled by Docker’s MCP Gateway. If an agent connects directly to a remote MCP server from inside a sandbox, that connection falls under the sandbox’s network policy instead. With the environment constrained and tool access governed, we can answer the second question: What can the agent do? Audit + Visibility: Can We See What Happened? Setting a policy is only part of the job. Security teams also need to know when that policy was applied, what action triggered it, and whether the action was allowed or denied. Docker AI Governance records sandbox policy decisions and sandbox session events as structured audit records. Each record captures details such as the principal, action, target, decision, and time. The records contain governance metadata rather than the contents of prompts or agent responses. Audit records can be kept locally or delivered to the cloud. With cloud delivery enabled, teams can search the organization-wide record, export it for further analysis, or forward events into existing SIEM (security information and event management) workflows. Denied actions are especially useful. A team can see not only that an action failed, but that a governance rule blocked it and why. Allowed decisions matter too: they provide a record of how policy was applied while the agent was working. Current audit coverage includes Docker Sandboxes policy decisions and sandbox session events. The same schema can support additional Docker AI sources as they become available. That closes the third part of the governance loop: Can we see what happened? A Trusted Software Supply Chain: Docker Hardened Images AI Governance controls access around the agent at runtime. There is a separate question that matters to the workflows those agents participate in: what container images and software artifacts are they building, testing, or deploying? Docker Hardened Images provide minimal, secure, and production-ready container images, Helm charts, and system packages maintained by Docker. In practical terms, this gives teams evidence about what is inside an image and how that image was produced. Docker Hardened Images include signed SBOMs, VEX information, cryptographic signatures, and SLSA Build Level 3 provenance. Instead of simply trusting where an image came from, teams can inspect what is inside it and verify information about how it was built. For organizations with additional compliance requirements, Docker also provides FIPS-enabled and STIG-ready variants through relevant DHI offerings. These capabilities sit alongside the broader DHI security and supply-chain controls rather than making any single standard the foundation by itself. AI Governance and Docker Hardened Images solve different parts of the trust problem. Governance controls the authority an agent has while it works; DHI helps establish trust in the container artifacts that the workflow depends on. Figure 2: Docker Hardened Images combine minimal container images with signed supply-chain metadata and verifiable build provenance. Putting the Three Layers Together Consider a developer using a coding agent to investigate an issue, update a service, and use an approved internal tool along the way. The agent begins inside a Docker Sandbox. It can work with the project and run the commands needed for the task, but its access is still bounded by policy. If it tries to reach a network destination or mount a host path that the organization has not allowed, the applicable sandbox policy can block that access. Now suppose the agent needs an MCP tool to look up information from another service. The request goes through Docker’s MCP Gateway, where organization policy determines whether that server and tool are permitted. A routine lookup might be allowed, while a more sensitive tool call could require confirmation or remain unavailable altogether. For governance activity currently covered by AI Governance Audit Logs, Docker records the policy decision and relevant session metadata. Security teams can see who initiated the activity, what policy-controlled action was evaluated, and whether it was allowed or denied. Those records can then feed the organization’s existing monitoring and SIEM workflow. If that same agent builds or tests a containerized application, the software entering the workflow matters too. Docker Hardened Images provide a more verifiable software foundation for that workflow, while AI Governance controls what the agent is authorized to do at runtime. The model is still making decisions about how to complete the task. What changes is the authority around those decisions. The agent can work autonomously inside the boundaries the organization has defined, while access outside those boundaries remains a policy decision. That is the practical value of the three layers working together: Sandbox Policies define where the agent can operate. MCP Tool Governance defines what tools it can use. Audit + Visibility shows how governed activity was handled. Taken together, the pattern is straightforward: define the boundary, check it before the agent starts working, enforce it while the agent is running, and use the resulting audit trail to understand what happened. If a boundary needs to change, the policy changes, not the expectation that the model will simply behave differently. Autonomy Without Unbounded Authority The challenge with agentic AI is not simply that agents can make decisions. It is that those decisions can now lead directly to actions. That makes the boundary around the agent just as important as the model itself. Docker AI Governance addresses that boundary through Sandbox Policies, MCP Tool Governance, and Audit + Visibility: controlling where agents can operate, what tools they can use, and how governed activity is recorded. Docker Hardened Images address a related supply-chain concern by helping teams work with smaller, verifiable container artifacts. The goal is not to remove autonomy from agents. It is to make sure autonomy does not automatically come with unlimited authority. As agents take on more real work, that distinction will matter more and more.
