title: [Amazon AWS] Test your applications against AWS locally with AWS Emulator
summary: Today we’re announcing AWS Emulator, a local emulator for Amazon Web Services (AWS) that you run on your machine. The AWS Command Line Interface (AWS CLI), the AWS SDKs, and your coding agents speak to it over a local HTTPS endpoint using the same AWS APIs they would use in the cloud, from your laptop. AWS Emulator has no additional service fee. You pay only for AWS resources when you deploy on AWS. Its source is on GitHub. You install it from an RPM or Debian package on Linux, and on macOS and Windows you run it in Docker. How it works You install the emulator, start it, and point your tools at the local endpoint. When AWS Emulator starts, it generates its own credentials, a config file, and a certificate, and writes them to ~/.aws/emulator/9297/. You set environment variables so the AWS SDK talks to your laptop instead of AWS, and your application code stays unchanged. From there, your existing tests, CLI scripts, and coding agents keep working the way they already do. A unit test that creates an Amazon DynamoDB table, writes an item, and reads it back is the same test, and it runs on your machine without a deployment. A coding agent can create resources, check the result, and iterate again without waiting on a deployment in a Region. The emulator is implemented in Rust so that it stays light on CPU and memory on a laptop. It supports the APIs of AWS services that have an API model in the AWS API models repository on GitHub, and because it’s built from those models, the same ones the AWS SDKs use, your requests and the errors you get back have the same shape as on AWS. If you are a developer, especially one working with coding agents such as Kiro or Claude Code, you can use that loop to test AWS interactions of real complexity locally. Let’s try it out To get started, I installed the package on Amazon Linux 2023. The package adds the aws-emulator command to /usr/bin/, so it’s on the path. PKG=https://downloads.aws.com/aws-emulator/packages/aws-emulator/LTS/latest sudo dnf install -y $PKG/aws-emulator-x86_64.rpm aws-emulator -v On macOS and Windows, you build a Docker image from the short Dockerfile in the documentation and run the emulator in a container. We don’t publish a ready-made image. I started the emulator with aws-emulator. It serves HTTPS on 127.0.0.1:9297, so only my own computer can reach it, and it writes its log as JSON lines that show the address, the config file, and the certificate file. aws-emulator In another terminal, I set the environment variables that point the AWS CLI at the emulator, and unset any variables that could supply real AWS credentials. export AWS_ENDPOINT_URL=https://127.0.0.1:9297 export AWS_SHARED_CREDENTIALS_FILE=~/.aws/emulator/9297/emulator_credentials export AWS_CONFIG_FILE=~/.aws/emulator/9297/config export AWS_EC2_METADATA_DISABLED=true export AWS_DISABLE_HOST_PREFIX_INJECTION=true export AWS_REGION=us-east-1 export AWS_DEFAULT_REGION=us-east-1 unset AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY AWS_SESSION_TOKEN AWS_PROFILE The emulator generates new keys each time it starts. Its access key IDs start with EMULATOR, so you can’t mistake them for real AWS keys, and it rejects requests signed with any other keys. To confirm that my shell was talking to the emulator, I checked the health endpoint and the caller identity. The emulator uses a single account, 000000000000. curl --cacert ~/.aws/emulator/9297/ca.pem https://127.0.0.1:9297/__admin/health aws sts get-caller-identity Then I created a bucket, copied in a small object, and listed it. $ aws s3 mb s3://local-getting-started make_bucket: local-getting-started $ echo "hello from the emulator" > hello.txt $ aws s3 cp hello.txt s3://local-getting-started/ upload: ./hello.txt to s3://local-getting-started/hello.txt $ aws s3 ls s3://local-getting-started/ With the AWS CLI pointed at my laptop, I had the same commands I already use and a local endpoint that answered them. Next I wanted to see it the way I actually work now, so with the emulator still running I opened Kiro and asked it to create an Amazon DynamoDB table, write an item, and read it back, all against AWS Emulator rather than my AWS account. kiro> Using the local AWS Emulator (the environment variables are already set in this shell), create a DynamoDB table "kiro-demo" with a string key "id", put an item {id: "item-1", msg: "hello from kiro"}, then read it back with get-item. $ aws dynamodb create-table --table-name kiro-demo \ --attribute-definitions AttributeName=id,AttributeType=S \ --key-schema AttributeName=id,KeyType=HASH \ --billing-mode PAY_PER_REQUEST $ aws dynamodb put-item --table-name kiro-demo \ --item '{"id": {"S": "item-1"}, "msg": {"S": "hello from kiro"}}' $ aws dynamodb get-item --table-name kiro-demo --key '{"id": {"S": "item-1"}}' To use the same setup with an existing test suite, I would start the emulator, set the same environment variables in the script that runs the tests, and run them as usual. Using the emulator in process Running the emulator as a local process gives you an HTTPS endpoint that works with the AWS CLI and the AWS SDKs through environment variables. Some SDKs need an extra setting to trust the emulator certificate, for example a trust store for the AWS SDK for Java. For tests, there is a second option. AWS Emulator ships an embedded mode that you instantiate directly inside your test process and wire into the SDK through its HTTP client, rather than talking to a separate server over the network. Each embedded instance keeps its own state, so tests do not share buckets, tables, or queues, and you can run many of them in parallel. Embedded mode is available for the AWS SDK for Rust. You add the aws-emulator-embedded crate from GitHub to the  section of your Cargo.toml file. The following example creates an Amazon DynamoDB table, writes an item, and reads it back, entirely in process. use aws_emulator_embedded::{AwsEmulatorEmbedded, EmbeddedOptions}; use aws_sdk_dynamodb::types::{ AttributeDefinition, AttributeValue, BillingMode, KeySchemaElement, KeyType, ScalarAttributeType, }; # async fn put_then_get_returns_the_item() { let emulator = AwsEmulatorEmbedded::new(EmbeddedOptions::default()); let config = aws_config::defaults(aws_config::BehaviorVersion::latest()) .http_client(emulator.http_client()) .region(aws_config::Region::new("us-east-1")) .credentials_provider(emulator.aws_credentials_provider()) .load() .await; let ddb = aws_sdk_dynamodb::Client::new(&config); ddb.create_table() .table_name("emulator-demo-table") .attribute_definitions( AttributeDefinition::builder() .attribute_name("id").attribute_type(ScalarAttributeType::S) .build().unwrap()) .key_schema( KeySchemaElement::builder() .attribute_name("id").key_type(KeyType::Hash) .build().unwrap()) .billing_mode(BillingMode::PayPerRequest) .send().await.unwrap(); ddb.put_item() .table_name("emulator-demo-table") .item("id", AttributeValue::S("item-1".into())) .item("msg", AttributeValue::S("hi".into())) .send().await.unwrap(); let got = ddb.get_item() .table_name("emulator-demo-table") .key("id", AttributeValue::S("item-1".into())) .send().await.unwrap(); assert_eq!(got.item().unwrap().get("msg").unwrap().as_s().unwrap(), "hi"); } When it runs as a local process, the emulator requires every request to be signed with Signature Version 4 (SigV4), the same way AWS does, and it exposes a /__admin/health endpoint on the same port so a script or a container can wait until it is ready before running tests. By default it also sends anonymous usage and error data, and you can turn it off. How we measure fidelity An emulator is only useful if a test that passes against it would also pass against AWS, so we measure that directly with fidelity tests. A fidelity test is a short program that uses an AWS SDK to run a workflow, such as storing an object and then reading and deleting it, and asserts how AWS behaves. We verify each fidelity test against real AWS. A fidelity test passes only if the emulator matches AWS on the response to every call, including the status code, the body, and the exact error code and message, and on the resources and data that the workflow creates. With each release, we publish how many fidelity tests pass for each service, as k of n. For example, 40 of 50 means that 40 of the service’s 50 fidelity tests pass. The set of fidelity tests is public in the aws-emulator-evaluation-suite repository on GitHub, including the ones that don’t pass yet, so you can see what we verified and run the fidelity tests yourself. Read a score as a snapshot of a product that’s improving. When we add fidelity tests, a score can go down even while the emulator gets better. If the emulator doesn’t implement an operation yet, it returns HTTP 501 (Not Implemented), so your tests fail right away. If the emulator acts differently from AWS, you can tell us by opening an issue in the AWS Emulator repository on GitHub. How the emulator is built AWS Emulator is built and maintained by agents from the AWS API models using Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Runtime Instances, AWS CodePipeline, and AWS CodeCommit, so it stays current with AWS as those models change. One group of agents looks for gaps, both by comparing emulator responses against real AWS and by statically comparing the emulator’s code against the published Smithy models, and files an issue for each gap it finds. Another group picks up an issue, writes tests, implements the behavior, and reviews the change for correctness, performance, and security. When the change is ready, it is pushed to a source repository, and that push triggers an AWS CodePipeline run that runs the fidelity tests before the change is published to the public GitHub repository. How we keep it secure Because the code is written by agents, an independent security agent reviews changes adversarially, both while the fix is being made and again in the release pipeline as a final check before anything ships. Security of your own use remains a shared responsibility. We build the emulator to run safely on your machine: it listens only on your own computer by default and rejects requests that aren’t signed with its own keys. You decide where it runs, what data you put in it, and how you test before production. Don’t use the emulator to test whether your application is secure. It doesn’t evaluate AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) policies and resource-based policies the way AWS does, so a request that AWS denies might succeed in the emulator. Keep real credentials out of the environment of your test jobs, and test your security settings and your whole application on AWS before you go to production. Now available AWS Emulator is generally available today. It has no additional service fee. You pay only for AWS resources when you deploy on AWS. You can install it from RPM or Debian packages on Linux, run it in Docker on macOS and Windows, or build from source, and it works with the AWS SDKs and the AWS CLI once you set environment variables. At launch, it has some limits. It doesn’t evaluate IAM policies the way AWS does, and each emulator acts as a single account, with no cross-account or cross-Region behavior. How closely it matches AWS varies by service and feature. To see how well the emulator covers the services that you use, check the fidelity scores in the AWS Emulator documentation. If you want to check regional availability, visit the AWS Capabilities by Region page in AWS Builder Center. If you want to call APIs, search documentation, find regional availability, and check troubleshooting about this new feature, try using the AWS MCP Server and plugins with your preferred AI tool. To get started, visit the AWS Emulator repository on GitHub and see the AWS Emulator documentation. Updated on November 12, 2026: Added links to the AWS Emulator repository on GitHub.

title: [HashiCorp] Nomad in 2026: A Year of Scale, Security, and Ecosystem Velocity
summary:
The future of orchestration is heterogeneous. Platform teams should not have to choose between containers, raw binaries, and virtual machines, or maintain separate, siloed control planes for each. Today’s infrastructure demands an orchestration platform that pairs high-throughput scheduling with granular kernel-level security and clean operational automation across them. This year, engineering across the Nomad ecosystem has focused on advancing that foundation. Spanning the Nomad 2.0 and 2.1 release cycles, from core consensus and performance enhancements to new scheduling governance, runtime drivers, autoscaling, and Terraform tooling, Nomad continues to evolve to meet the demands of modern production environments. Improve control plane performance and recovery Nomad 2.0 lets operators migrate the Raft log store from BoltDB to a Write-Ahead Log (WAL) backend, which offers better performance for write-heavy workloads. Nomad 2.0.5 added the plan_apply_pipeline setting, which lets operators control how many outstanding plans the leader allows when evaluating plans. For recovery, Nomad 2.1 adds nomad operator snapshot filter. It removes selected entries from a snapshot and writes the result to a copy. Operators can use it to clean up a snapshot before restoring it, or to remove a large number of pending evaluations when recovering a cluster from an outage. Govern high-volume batch bursts with node pool queueing High-volume batch bursts, like automated pipelines or ML inference, can leave smaller jobs stuck behind larger ones when capacity runs short. Nomad 2.1 introduces the experimental Batch Job Queue to give operators greater control over how batch jobs are scheduled within node pools. The queue holds pending batch jobs and provides two queueing options, FIFO, and a dynamic priority implementation which adjusts the priority of queued jobs based on multiple configurable factors. This helps prevent tenant starvation and supports fair-share scheduling. Advance containerless security and storage with Driver exec2 exec2 v0.2.0 brings container-grade capabilities to non-containerized workloads, adding Linux ambient capabilities, Host and CSI volume mounts, and nomad alloc exec support without container daemon overhead. The exec2 task driver leverages native Linux kernel namespaces and Landlock filesystem sandboxing to isolate raw binary tasks. With v0.2.0, operators can selectively grant Linux ambient capabilities using allow_caps, cap_add, and cap_drop — a web service can bind privileged ports via CAP_NET_BIND_SERVICE while dropping all other root privileges. exec2 tasks can now mount persistent storage via standard Nomad Host and CSI volume blocks, native nomad alloc exec support enables interactive shell debugging and script-based health checks, and memory telemetry transitions to modern Linux standards, accurately reporting Resident Set Size (RSS) under cgroups v2. Expand workload diversity with rootless Podman and virtual machines Orchestration flexibility extends beyond containers and binaries to include rootless environments and virtual machines: Rootless Podman (v0.6.5): Nomad Driver Podman 0.6.5 streamlines its dependency footprint by removing transitive Docker Go packages while adding multi-architecture platform overrides (os, arch, variant), direct HTTP(S) image archive loading, and shared IPC namespaces for inter-task /dev/shm communication. Virtual Machine Orchestration with Virt (Tech Preview): The Virt Task Driver v0.0.2-beta.1 (Tech Preview) advances native virtual machine orchestration on Nomad, adding support for host directory and Ceph storage pools, block-device volume attachments, and macvtap network interfaces. Strengthen infrastructure resilience with APM-driven autoscaling and fail-safe drains Effective autoscaling requires both application-aware metrics and fail-safe teardowns. Relying solely on CPU or memory thresholds often lags behind real traffic surges, while aggressive node scale-in risks terminating instances before draining tasks have fully stopped. Nomad Autoscaler v0.6.0 and v0.5.0 address both. New native APM plugins for Instana (v0.6.0) and InfluxDB (v0.5.0), alongside Prometheus instant query support (query_window = "instant"), let teams drive scaling decisions directly from application metrics. Schedule blocks let you define time-based windows to proactively warm capacity ahead of predictable events. On lifecycle safety, v0.6.0 fixes a critical gap: the autoscaler now waits until all tasks on a drained node have fully stopped before issuing termination commands, preventing long-running shutdown hooks or background workers from being interrupted prematurely. Simplify GitOps and eliminate state secrets with Terraform provider v2.6.1 Managing Nomad jobs declaratively with Terraform is standard practice for modern platform teams. Two friction points have consistently come up: sensitive ACL tokens and variables persisting in Terraform state files, and Terraform applies overwriting dynamic task replica counts managed by the Nomad Autoscaler. Terraform Provider v2.6.1 addresses both. Ephemeral Resources allow CI/CD pipelines to generate short-lived Nomad ACL tokens, client intro tokens, and variables on the fly, utilizing them during execution without storing sensitive secrets in permanent Terraform state. The preserve_counts parameter ensures that Terraform applies update job specifications, container images, and configurations without overwriting dynamic scaling counts established by the Nomad Autoscaler. Combined with new nomad_node and nomad_nodes data sources for dynamic topology inspection, platform teams achieve clean, conflict-free GitOps automation. Nomad ecosystem releases at a glance The following matrix summarizes the recent releases across the Nomad platform and ecosystem: Component Version Key Operational & Architectural Value Nomad Platform v2.1.1 / v2.0.5 Batch Job Queue, raft-WAL store, plan_apply_pipeline, Snapshot Filtering Nomad Autoscaler v0.6.0 / v0.5.0 Instana & InfluxDB APM plugins, scheduled scaling windows, safe node termination Driver exec2 v0.2.0 Ambient Linux capabilities, CSI & Host volume mounts, alloc exec Driver Podman v0.6.5 Multi-arch overrides, HTTP(S) image transport, shared IPC, streamlined dependencies Driver Virt v0.0.2-beta.1 Native VM orchestration (Tech Preview) - Ceph/directory storage pools, block storage, macvtap Terraform Provider v2.6.1 Ephemeral secret resources, preserve_counts for seamless autoscaling, node data sources

Get started with Nomad 2.1 These releases reflect our ongoing focus: providing platform engineering teams with a reliable, flexible orchestrator that scales smoothly across any workload type. title: [CNCF] How to support your app on Kubernetes environments you don’t control
summary: Running an application in Kubernetes is one thing, but supporting that application in Kubernetes environments your customers run is something else entirely. You don’t control the cluster configuration, its upgrade schedule, the surrounding tooling, or the process for investigating an incident. But customers will still look to you when your application won’t install, an upgrade breaks, or a workload behaves differently in their environment than they expected. That doesn’t mean customer-managed Kubernetes deployments can’t work, but it does mean support has to account for the variation you’ll see in real clusters. No Two Customer Environments Are Alike You’ll definitely have two customers (or more!) who both say they run Kubernetes and yet have very different environments. One may run a managed Kubernetes service in a public cloud. Another may operate its own infrastructure. They may use different Kubernetes versions, networking configurations, ingress controllers, storage classes, image registries, security policies, observability tools, or access controls. Those differences affect how your application deploys and how your team supports it. A chart that installs cleanly in your reference architecture may fail because a customer’s admission policies reject a required permission, their storage configuration doesn’t meet your application’s requirements, or their cluster runs a Kubernetes version you haven’t tested yet or no longer support. Unfortunately, your customer still experiences that as a problem with your application. That’s why your team needs a documented view of what the application requires from the cluster, and what falls outside the support boundary. At a minimum, customers need to know: Which Kubernetes versions and distributions you support Which permissions, policies, and cluster capabilities the application needs What networking, ingress, DNS, certificate, secret management, and storage configuration the application expects What resources the application needs to run reliably Which logs, events, metrics, and configuration details your support team will need during an escalation. With bonus points for providing commands directly. The goal isn’t to make every customer environment identical (you can’t). Instead, you need to define a supported operating model so every deployment doesn’t turn into a new discovery process for your customer support team. Customers Won’t Upgrade on Your Schedule Your application roadmap may assume customers will move to newer Kubernetes versions quickly. A quick reality check: most won’t. Customers have their own release schedules, validation processes, maintenance windows, compliance requirements, internal dependencies, and risk thresholds. Even when they want to upgrade, their platform team may have a long list of cluster add-ons, integrations, and workloads to validate first. Like any other software, Kubernetes and different components in its ecosystem change over time. APIs are deprecated and removed, version compatibility varies across control-plane and node components, and the upstream project supports release branches for only the three most recent minor releases. Your team needs a compatibility policy that answers a few basic questions: Which Kubernetes versions do you support today? Which versions are approaching the end of support? How much notice do customers get before you stop supporting a version? What does a customer need to do if an application release depends on a newer Kubernetes capability? Can you offer a documented workaround when a customer can’t upgrade immediately? If the answer to every compatibility problem is to update Kubernetes, customers will quickly find that your support isn’t aligned with how they operate. Your team needs to explain what’s incompatible, why it matters, and the easiest path to return to a supported configuration. Kubernetes Expertise Has to Be Customer-Facing A general application support team can’t diagnose every Kubernetes issue. When a product runs inside a cluster your customer manages, customer-facing teams need enough Kubernetes depth to identify where the problem really lives. That doesn’t mean every support employee has to operate production clusters. It does mean someone working directly with customers needs to understand the difference between an application issue, a deployment-configuration issue, and a cluster-level issue. For example, a pod stuck in Pending may point to unavailable capacity, resource requests that don’t fit on available nodes, a scheduling constraint, or a policy that prevents placement. An image pull failure may involve registry access, credentials, network connectivity, or image policy enforcement. Those details determine who needs to take the next action and what evidence they need to act on it. Your customer-facing team needs dedicated Kubernetes expertise that can: Ask for the right diagnostic information early Review Kubernetes events, pod status, and relevant logs Identify when a customer platform, security, networking, or infrastructure team needs to get involved Explain the issue in terms each stakeholder can act on Escalate to engineering with enough environmental context to investigate effectively Getting accurate answers to these questions matters because the person opening a support case may not own the cluster. The application team probably owns the deployment. A platform team probably owns Kubernetes. Security owns policies. Another infrastructure team may own networking, storage, or identity. Someone on your team needs to help move the issue between those groups. Build for Variation You can’t control every Kubernetes environment where customers run your application. You can control whether your support model treats that variation as expected or as a surprise. So make sure you have a plan for it by: Defining what you support. Documenting the requirements that matter. Testing the Kubernetes versions and deployment conditions you commit to supporting. Setting a clear upgrade and deprecation policy. Making Kubernetes expertise available during onboarding, deployment, escalation, and ongoing support. The support model changes when a provider manages the Kubernetes layer alongside the customer. Instead of troubleshooting an application across an unknown mix of cluster configurations, versions, networking, and add-ons, the provider and customer can work from a more clearly defined operating foundation. title: [CNCF] Optimizing Kubernetes admission control: Where Kyverno’s CEL admission cost actually goes
summary: Kyverno’s CEL (Common Expression Language)-based engines exist to evaluate policy expressions. So when we profiled the admission path, we expected to find the bulk of the cost in CEL evaluation. It was not there. About 86% of what the engine allocated went into preparing the object for evaluation, and almost none of it into evaluating policy. We went looking because a public benchmark put Kyverno behind the alternatives. Those benchmarks measured the legacy ClusterPolicy JMESPath engine, which did have a real regression at the time, and the usual answer was to point people at the newer CEL-based engine instead. That answer was right but incomplete: we had not checked what the CEL engine itself was spending its time on. This post is about where that performance cost came from, why it grew with the number of policies you deploy, and what removing it did. The fix ships in Kyverno 1.19.2. Please read the limitations section before you quote any number here. And as always, run your own tests in your environments, for real-world accuracy. What the profile showed Kyverno’s CEL engines evaluate policies against a CEL activation: a set of variables your policy expressions can reference. One of those variables is request, the AdmissionRequest the API server sent, converted into the unstructured map form CEL understands. Here is a heap profile of the ValidatingPolicy engine handling admission requests, before and after the change, by share of total allocated bytes: Before, ConvertObjectToUnstructured accounted for 86.8% of everything the engine allocated. CEL evaluation itself barely registered. After, object conversion falls to 2.9%, and the largest single frame becomes evaluateWithData — the code that actually runs your policy expressions. The same pattern shows up in the MutatingPolicy engine, which was paying a smaller but still substantial version of the same cost: One caveat on reading those profiles: the post-fix benchmark completes more iterations in the same time because it is faster, so the two profiles have different absolute totals. Compare the shares, not the raw bytes. Per-request figures come from the benchmark table further down. Why: the same object, converted once per policy The API server sends the admitted object as raw JSON bytes. CEL cannot read bytes, so Kyverno parses them into the map form CEL understands before it can evaluate anything against them. That conversion happened inside the loop over matched policies rather than before it. With the Pod Security Standards set, roughly 16 policies match a typical Pod creation — so Kyverno parsed the same Pod 16 times, same input, same output, every time. The cost grew with your policy count and with the size of the object being admitted: O(policies), where it should have been O(1). The object does not change between policies. There was never a reason to convert it more than once. The fix: convert once per request The change moves the conversion out of the per-policy loop. Kyverno builds the CEL request value once, before the loop starts, and every matched policy reuses it. Doing that without changing what policies see takes some care. The expensive part of the conversion is the admitted object itself, so Kyverno converts a copy of the request with that object temporarily blanked out — which leaves only cheap fields to walk — and splices the object back in afterwards. The same conversion code still produces the result, so the output matches what policies saw before rather than being a reimplementation that someone has to keep in sync by hand. Keeping policy behavior identical The first attempt used a single shared builder for every CEL engine. Testing caught that this quietly changed how policies behave, because the engines had never agreed on what request.object meant in the first place. Validating and generating policies saw the object exactly as the API server sent it. Mutating policies saw a normalized version. The two also disagreed about what an empty object looks like to CEL, which matters for operations like DELETE where one side is absent. Unifying them would have changed the result of expressions people already have deployed. That is a conversation worth having, but not one a performance fix should start on its own. So each engine keeps the contract it already had, sharing one fast implementation underneath. Equivalence tests pin this down: they run the original code as the reference and compare its output against the new one field by field, across every request type, so any drift fails the build. What changed The benchmark calls the engine directly with a roughly 50 KB Pod and a varying number of matched policies. It times the engine alone — building the request value, matching, and evaluating CEL. It does not include the webhook round trip, the API server, or etcd, so these are not end-to-end admission latencies. Matched policiesAllocations beforeAllocations afterEngine time beforeEngine time after12,3278540.31 ms0.10 ms1637,0552,7184.91 ms0.16 ms64148,1318,67220.01 ms0.36 ms The MutatingPolicy engine improves on the same curve, from 258,943 to 52,689 allocations and 10.59 ms to 2.97 ms at 64 policies. The slope is the point, not the headline multiple. Before the change, allocations grew about 63 times going from 1 policy to 64. After, about 10 times — and that residual growth is CEL evaluation, which is the work you deployed the policies to get. Object preparation is now constant per request instead of proportional to how many policies you run. Practically: adding policies to a Kyverno deployment used to carry a hidden per-policy serialization cost on top of the evaluation you asked for. It no longer does. Image verification too The image verification engine had the same pattern, with its own private copy of the conversion code, so it got the same fix. The gain there is memory rather than speed: image verification spends most of its time fetching signatures and attestations over the network, and that part does not change. How this compares to native admission policies With the per-policy tax gone, it is worth asking where Kyverno’s CEL engine actually sits against the API server’s own ValidatingAdmissionPolicy. Running the same 16 Pod Security Standards policies through both engines on one cluster, the answer depends on how many policies you enforce: At one policy, native is ahead: about 9.2 ms against Kyverno’s 12.8 ms. At the full 16-policy set, Kyverno is ahead: about 20 ms against native’s 29 ms. Those numbers were measured on Kyverno 1.19.0, which predates the change described above. The Kyverno side of that chart should now be better than shown; we have not re-run the comparison. The two engines pay their costs differently. Native dispatches each policy separately on the API server, so its cost grows with the number of policies you enforce. Kyverno pays once per request to receive the object over a webhook, and that cost is shared across however many policies then evaluate. With only a policy or two, native is ahead. Once you are running a realistic set, Kyverno matches it and can come out ahead. That framing only became accurate with this fix. Kyverno’s cost was not fixed per request before it — it was per policy, which is exactly why the curve looked the way it did. The CPU side is more one-sided. Under matched load, Kyverno’s engine used about 3.2 cores against the API server’s 8.2 for native. The surprise in the API server profile is that 67% of its CPU sits in the policy dispatch machinery while the actual CEL bytecode execution is about 5.5% — the cost is dispatching 16 policies and building an input for each, not evaluating them. And that load lands on the control plane, which you cannot scale horizontally the way you can scale a Kyverno deployment. Both numbers come from a single-host setup where the webhook hop is loopback and effectively free. On a real multi-node cluster that hop costs real latency on every Kyverno request, which narrows the latency gap and matters most at low policy counts. The CPU finding does not depend on topology. The legacy engine, briefly The benchmarks that prompted this work measured ClusterPolicy, the older non-CEL engine, so it is worth saying what happened there. We reproduced the regression across four releases, each on a fresh cluster, run in shuffled order over eight rounds so no version was systematically favored, and compared everything against 1.13.6. The regression is real — between 12% and 23% depending on load — and it appears between 1.16.4 and 1.17.0. That is where the engine started copying its entire evaluation context on every checkpoint, in order to fix a separate bug where one rule’s data could leak into the next. The fix keeps that guarantee but stops paying for it upfront: it takes a shallow snapshot and only copies a value when something actually writes to it. The benchmark returns to roughly its pre-regression level, and the rule isolation still holds, pinned by a test that fails on the old code. This ships in 1.19.2 alongside the CEL work, and only there. The legacy engine is on its way out, so the effort belongs in the engine replacing it. What this does not fix The engine still pays one JSON round-trip of the admitted object per request, to preserve the raw, un-normalized parse that request.object has always exposed. Evaluating against the typed object, or a cheaper representation, would remove even that — but it would change what policies see, so it needs its own design. Mutating policies thread full objects between policies rather than propagating a patch diff. A patch-only model is a substantially larger redesign and is not implemented. Tail latency under sustained load on a single replica is not addressed by any of this, and we have not re-measured it since. If you have seen Kyverno’s p95 swing widely between runs at high load, that is a separate problem and it is still open. Limitations Single machine. Everything here reproduces the relationship between configurations, not the absolute numbers you would see on a 32-core server. Most of this is a Go benchmark. The allocation and timing figures come from benchmarks driving the real engine loop, and the profiles come from those benchmark runs. They isolate the engine cleanly, and they exclude network, serialization at the webhook boundary, and etcd. The engine comparison uses loopback, so the webhook network hop is excluded, and dry-run, so the etcd write is excluded. The native side runs Kyverno’s generated policies, which is a faithful same-policy comparison rather than a hand-tuned native policy set. Side controllers were disabled in these runs. Only the admission controller was active. Reproduce it The harness is in the Kyverno repository under docs/perf-testing/: the version ladder, the pinned Pod Security Standards policy set, the k6 scripts, and the cluster setup. The engine benchmarks live beside the code they measure, in pkg/cel/policies/vpol/engine and pkg/engine/context. If you benchmark Kyverno and get a result you do not like, please publish it — with the method, the caveats, and the per-trial numbers. Conclusion Our mission at Kyverno is to be the best policy engine for Kubernetes and beyond. Admission control is a critical process in Kubernetes clusters, and a slow or misconfigured controller can impact cluster operations. Thanks to our community, we have fixed performance issues and added more tests. For future releases, we will be looking at improving concurrency and further optimization. Thanks to Mustafa Erdinç, whose comparison of different Kubernetes policy engines motivated this work. title: [Pulumi] Introducing Pulumi Delivery: your release pipeline as code
summary: Coding agents have made writing software faster than shipping it. The bottleneck is now everything after the code: release pipelines full of bespoke scripts, console steps, and hand-run promotions that slow teams down and don’t scale. Today, we’re introducing Pulumi Delivery, available in public preview. With Delivery, you define how a change moves from development through staging to production in the same languages you already use for infrastructure: TypeScript, Python, Go, HCL, YAML, and more. Your pipeline becomes a Pulumi program, so it gets the same policies and review process as the rest of your infrastructure, whether a person or an agent wrote the change. The new bottleneck Most applications span many infrastructure stacks. For example, your service may have separate stacks per environment for its networking layer, database, and application code, and they need to be deployed in the correct order. Today, that ordering and the rest of your delivery logic live in standalone pipeline files and manual console steps. Those tools run separately from your infrastructure, your secrets, and your policies, so the rules you enforce on a stack often don’t apply to the pipeline that deploys it. Reusing logic across services usually means copying YAML, and testing a pipeline usually means running it and watching. Agents make that gap wider. They’re fluent in code, but the context needed to promote a release is scattered across consoles and config files they can’t see or access. Delivery puts your release pipeline in the same code your agents already work in, so you can ship as fast as they write. Your delivery pipeline, as code A Delivery pipeline is a Pulumi program. In it, you declare the repositories you deploy from, the stages a release moves through, the stacks each stage updates, and the gates that hold a release. Pulumi Cloud then runs each release through those stages in order. Here’s a pipeline that deploys a shop app from dev through staging to prod, and waits for approval before production: import * as delivery from "@pulumi/delivery"; const repo = new delivery_git_hub_source.repo, directory = "network" } app = { stack = "shop-app/${each.key}", source = delivery_git_hub_source.repo, directory = "app" } } } Once you register the pipeline, every push to main starts a new release. Delivery pins the release to that commit, so the code that passed in staging is exactly the code that reaches prod. Because a pipeline is a real program, you can express common patterns like promotion logic, canary rollouts, blue-green deployments, and multi-region sequencing as composable code. Write a rollout pattern once as a function, reuse it across services, and test it like any other code. One pipeline for all your stacks Getting the order right is what makes a release safe, and the more stacks you have, the harder it is to get right. Delivery uses what Pulumi already knows about your infrastructure to work out the order for you. When your app stack depends on a value from your network stack, such as a subnet ID, Delivery updates the network first and the app second, without you writing that order down anywhere. Stacks that don’t depend on each other update at the same time. You still set the big steps, such as dev, staging, and prod, yourself, and you can order individual stacks by hand when you need to. Gate releases with AI risk review Approval gates work well until the number of changes outgrows the number of people available to review them. With Delivery, you can add an AI reviewer as a gate. It assesses each change’s risk and either promotes the change or escalates it to a human for review. You can also gate releases on decision models such as TypeSafe’s Jev, which return a calibrated risk score. Your pipeline compares that score against a threshold you set, so routine changes move on their own and the risky ones wait for a person. You decide where that line sits, and you can move it as you build trust in the results. Turn production signals into reviewed fixes Delivery can also react to the observability tools you already have, including PagerDuty, Honeycomb, Sentry, and Datadog. When a signal points to a problem in production, an agent can prepare a fix and open a pull request under your policies. That fix then moves through the same pipeline as any other change, with the same gates at every stage. Agents get a fast path to production that’s also the governed one. Get started with Pulumi Delivery Pulumi Delivery is available today in public preview in the Free, Essentials, Pro, and Enterprise editions of Pulumi Cloud. To build your first pipeline, start with the Delivery documentation. We’d love to hear what you’re shipping with it. Share feedback in the Pulumi Community Slack or contact support.

title: [Microsoft Azure] Building the next generation of multimodal AI experiences with fal in Microsoft Foundry
summary: Microsoft and fal partner to expand video generation in Microsoft Foundry, helping developers bring creative ideas into enterprise applications.Video workloads do not all start with the same input or aim for the same result. A creative team might explore several interpretations of a written brief. A retailer might turn an approved product image into a short motion concept. An application developer might combine image generation and video generation into a workflow that takes an idea from description to frame to scene. Each scenario brings different requirements for visual quality, motion, creative control, turnaround time, and cost. All of this means that a multi-model solution is necessary to realize a full vision. Today, Microsoft and fal are helping developers find the right tools for their workloads. We are excited to announce that Kling, LTX, and MiniMax video models are rolling out to in public preview in Microsoft Foundry through our new partnership with fal. Available as a first-party Azure service, these text-to-video and image-to-video options give creators and developers more ways to utilize video generation with the experiences they want to build. The partnership expands the choices available in Microsoft Foundry while bringing video into the broader platform developers use to build AI applications. The goal is to let developers pick the right model for each step of an experience, then connect those steps into a working application. “fal has seen incredible adoption this year alone with generative media across all industries from advertising to marketing to gaming. Partnering with Microsoft allows both of us to truly enable the wide creative ecosystem and ensure that all AI solutions that lean on generative media, becomes a multi-model one.” – Burkay Gur, Cofounder Bringing fal’s generative media focus to enterprise buildersfal is the full stack for generative media, built for creators and developers, with APIs for over 1500 models across image, video, audio, 3D, and generative worlds. As a truly encapsulating platform, fal provides inference, training, and infrastructure to run generative media workloads in production, while also providing innovative post trained models that pushes the boundaries on speed and quality. That specialization matters because generative media is both a creative and an engineering workload. A compelling demo is only the start. Production applications also need to handle real traffic, scale with demand, and balance output quality, latency, and cost. Through this partnership, developers will be able to access a selected set of video models in Microsoft Foundry, served by fal and sourced from the companies that build them. The initial portfolio gives teams a choice of models for different creative requirements instead of relying on one model for every task, with more models planned over time. A portfolio for different video experiencesThe initial portfolio spans Kling v3 Pro, LTX-2.5 Fast, LTX-2.5 Pro, MiniMax H3 Max, and MiniMax H3 Max Turbo. These models give developers different starting points for generating video from text and animating existing images. A team rapidly exploring creative concepts may prioritize speed and cost, while a team producing fewer, higher-fidelity assets may weigh output quality more heavily. Whether an application starts from text or an existing image, and what it needs in output quality and cost, also shapes the choice. Kling: From a still image to a directed scene Kling v3 Pro combines cinematic visuals and fluid motion with native audio generation and custom element support. Its image-to-video capabilities give developers control over how a starting image becomes a moving scene, a fit for applications that prioritize visual direction and motion. LTX: One model for fast drafts, one for final output For rapid iteration and previews, LTX-2.5 Fast is the speed-optimized option; for high-fidelity final output, LTX-2.5 Pro is the quality-optimized option. Both support text-to-video and image-to-video generation with synchronized audio. MiniMax: Another approach to video generation MiniMax H3 Max and MiniMax H3 Max Turbo are post-trained variants of MiniMax H3 focused on prompt adherence, aesthetics, and inference performance. For developers, they provide additional options to evaluate against an application’s creative brief, quality requirements, and performance needs. “When building with video models, the details matter: how closely the output follows your prompt, how well it preserves your reference images/videos/audios and how quickly you can try another idea. Kling gives developers control over detailed reference to video generation. LTX offers fast iteration and high-quality output through its Fast and Pro variants. H3 Max brings fal’s post-training and inference optimizations to improve quality and speed. Having these models available through Microsoft Foundry gives developers more flexibility to choose what works best for the application they are building.” – Gökay Aydoğan, Creative Engineer Built for enterprise video workloadsBringing video generation into an enterprise application requires more than choosing the right model. Teams need a platform where they can evaluate different options, build with the models that fit their requirements, and operate those experiences alongside the rest of their applications. The initial portfolio of video models is hosted in the US, and Microsoft Foundry is the first provider to offer a US-hosted Kling endpoint. title: [Engineering at Meta] Intelligent Delivery: Making Every Unit of Compute Serve Better Ads
summary: Ads ranking models are growing toward LLM scale faster than the hardware to run them can keep up. An extra unit of compute has more impact on some ad requests, models, and chips than on others. The challenge is deciding where to allocate it to get the best outcome for the entire system. We built Intelligent Delivery, an ML-driven system that allocates resources across the serving stack toward the system-wide optimum. It has delivered ~10% incremental ranking performance on top of model and system advancements since 2017. We’re sharing a few of Intelligent Delivery’s capabilities: how we build ML models to predict the marginal utility of compute, multi-layered mechanisms to move resources across the system, and how we increasingly leverage agentic AI to continuously detect and respond to system shifts. As frontier ads ranking systems advance toward larger models, broader candidate sets, and richer delivery architectures, they also place greater demands on serving efficiency. Compute resources do not scale at the rate that models and system complexity do. The challenge is not just how to build more powerful models, but how to operate them efficiently across a heterogeneous system, with finite serving capacity, and under a tight latency budget. We recently shared how we put idle inference capacity to work. This post covers how we decide where each unit of compute goes to achieve globally optimal system efficiency. Intelligent Delivery is our approach to the problem, and it has contributed an additional ~10% improvement in ads ranking performance on top of model and system advancements across major surfaces, from 2017 through the first half of 2026. It introduces an ML-driven, increasingly AI-operated adaptive optimization layer that continuously directs resources toward the requests, models, hardware fleets, and ranking stages with the highest marginal utility. This helps us run advanced ads ranking models efficiently in production, getting more out of every unit of compute to serve better ads for people who use our apps and services. The Goal and What Makes It Difficult One of our goals is to create a delivery system that continuously converges on its global optimum, regardless of how user behavior changes, models evolve, and the serving stack grows more complex. Three fundamental properties of ads delivery systems make this challenging: The marginal impact of compute is highly heterogeneous and context-dependent: The same additional unit of compute can generate very different returns depending on the product surface, user intent, candidate quality, and system state. Request-aware signals alone are not sufficient; allocating well means estimating, for every request, the return on every available tunable system parameter, where each knob behaves differently at each stage of the funnel. We need to produce a per-request result calculation across a vast decision space within milliseconds. Local optimality does not translate to global optimality: Result estimation is just the start; the serving stack must also be dynamically controllable. Ads delivery spans multi-stage ranking, hundreds of models, generations of hardware, and many data centers. Resources cannot be shifted freely and reliably across these boundaries without adaptive controls that account for complex dependencies throughout the stack. The global optimum is a moving target: The optimization landscape is continuously shifting. Every new model, hardware generation, or new architecture changes the landscape and can invalidate previously optimal allocation decisions. The system needs to adapt quickly enough to retain its optimality. Intelligent Delivery includes three capabilities, each designed to address one of these fundamental system challenges. Capabilities of Intelligent Delivery 1. Request Understanding: A Shared ML Intelligence Layer for Compute Some ad requests benefit more from additional computation than others. Initially, we captured these differences through coarse segments: Requests were grouped by attributes such as surface, context, and ad creative representation, with engineers creating policies to allocate resources for each group. This approach delivered improvements but did not scale. Every new signal multiplied the rules, making the effort unsustainable, and independent segments could not capture the nonlinear interactions among thousands of signals, which limited accuracy. We achieved about a 20% improvement in identifying the highest-impact ad requests in offline benchmarks on major surfaces, relative to our previous production model, after reframing this into two ML problems: Which ad requests are most likely to benefit from additional compute? And how will different resource settings affect their outcomes and serving performance? A side-by-side comparison of static rule-based segmentation, where every request in a bucket gets the same compute, and signal-driven decisions, where an ML-driven predictor sets compute for each request. To answer the first question, we built the Resource Core Model, deep learning models with 6B sparse parameters and 20M dense parameters that run once before candidate retrieval and are shared across the delivery funnel. Learned embeddings and deep feature interactions capture nuanced request patterns that manually defined segments cannot. We then fine-tune the Resource Core Model into a set of specialized models, each generating incremental signals about outcome, compute consumption, and latency impact. Together this forms a shared ML intelligence layer for resource allocation: The Resource Core Model understands each request and its serving behavior, while individual mechanisms determine how to translate those predictions into actions. An architecture diagram of the Resource Core Model, showing how dense and sparse request features pass through stacked interaction layers to predict each request’s outcome, compute consumption, and latency impact. 2. Allocation Mechanisms: A Hierarchy of Decision Engines Ads serving runs on a globally distributed, heterogeneous fleet with many data center regions, several hardware generations, and millions of hosts, all shared by a multi-tier serving stack. A single allocation mechanism cannot control the complex resource distribution end to end. So we decomposed the problem into a hierarchy of layers and built a dedicated decision engine for each. The easiest way to see the hierarchy is to follow a single request through it. Someone opens their feed. An ad request is created, and over the next few hundred milliseconds it passes through a chain of resource allocation decisions. This leads us to three important questions and answers. Which region serves it? Traffic and capacity are not colocated, and each region carries a different hardware mix and a different amount of headroom — so the same unit of compute is more efficient in some places than in others. We built real-time infrastructure to dynamically shift traffic between regions in a cycle of minutes, driving toward the point where every region achieves the same level of efficiency on its marginal unit of capacity. What hardware does it land on? Our fleet spans CPUs from Intel, AMD, and Arm and accelerators from NVIDIA, AMD, and our own Meta Training and Inference Accelerator (MTIA), across several generations of each. The hard part isn’t the variety; it’s that capacity isn’t interchangeable. Our stages are bound by different resources — retrieval by memory capacity, ranking by compute, and model inference by accelerator throughput — so there is no single fastest SKU, only a best match per workload. We benchmark measured efficiency for every workload-SKU pair, then solve the assignment so that scarce hardware goes to the workloads that convert it into the most useful work. Inside the host, how much of this machine does the request get? Concurrent requests differ in latency budget and impact, under a hard tail-latency SLO. We predict each request’s expected outcome and its compute and latency cost in real time using our advanced deep learning models, and solve a constrained optimization that maximizes impact delivered within the host’s latency budget — as the host load increases, the performance trade-off rises and resource-intensive low-impact work is trimmed first. Enforcing those decisions takes control across the whole stack, so the framework spans from kernel-level scheduler up to application-level thread pools. A three-step flowchart following one ad request through the decision hierarchy: which region serves it, which hardware it runs on, and how much of the host it gets. These three steps are just a subset of the allocation decisions we make during a request’s lifecycle. Following this, we optimize the number of ads to rank for each request in each ranking stage, what ad candidates enter the pool, and much more. These allocation decisions are tightly coupled, so a resource change in any one of them ripples across the whole system. Shifting traffic between regions changes per-host load, which drives the feedback controller that sets how much work each request gets. We validate these changes in an end-to-end, closed-loop hardware testing environment to make sure we are optimizing for the global optimum instead of a local optimum. 3. Optimization Loop: Self-Optimizing Serving with Agentic AI As our ad system advances, productionizing a new model, a new mechanism, or new hardware into the system requires a lot of effort to achieve seamless integration. We can’t brute-force every single configuration across millions of tunable dimensions built in our system for a new change. That would require too much time and far more hardware resources than we have. We relied heavily on human expertise and engineers’ prior knowledge to identify promising configurations. But this approach didn’t scale, because every new model, mechanism, and hardware generation expanded the search space faster than engineers could explore it. We tried automating this with a constrained optimization approach, which delivered improvements but remained inflexible and slow. We found that it lacked the ability to generalize (it could only cover a few key knobs) and couldn’t effectively incorporate human intuition from prior experience. Instead of doing a blind search, AI agents continuously monitor the entire system landscape, identifying changes and inefficiencies to address. In a long context window, an agent reads mechanism source code, design documents, and a decade of experiment logs and narrows that to a handful of changes worth testing. Engineers review and approve the final change before it ships. Today, agents can already propose well-reasoned changes and design and run rigorous experiments. In the first half of 2026, agents contributed to about 20% of Intelligent Delivery optimizations. On our most automated mechanism, they now contribute to about 80% of the engineering effort, from understanding the system landscape and forming hypotheses to running experiments and converging on the final change. This shortens the optimization loop from months to weeks while keeping people firmly in control. And it steadily captures the expertise engineers have built over the years. A loop diagram of the AI-driven optimization cycle, where agents collect data, propose changes, and run experiments, with an engineer approving every change and a shared knowledge base feeding each step. The Next Frontiers for Intelligent Delivery End-to-end real-time optimization: Today, understanding a request and deciding how to serve it are still two separate steps. We’re building toward fusing them into a single model that reads a request and serves it in real time, without months of experiments. There’s established work in varying compute per request with learning-based methods. However, doing it jointly across every serving stage at once — under shifting traffic, hard capacity limits, and tight inter-stage dependencies — is the part that’s still open, and it’s what we’re pushing on. Serving state-of-the-art models on GPUs: Large ranking models, like Meta’s Generative Ads Model (GEM), are growing toward LLM scale and increasingly run on GPUs, which opens a different optimization space. GPU capacity doesn’t divide the way CPU time does — it comes in whole, fixed blocks, and throughput, batching, and memory all behave differently. The levers we built for a CPU world have to be reimagined, and much of our work now goes into understanding those mechanisms and turning them into new levers. The more useful work we get out of each accelerator, the more people we can serve with strong models under the same capacity.
